headline: Monhegan mackerel and Boothbay bluefish: warm water pushes a southern fish north
subhead: Snapper blues we flagged two weeks back are turning into keeper-class fish in the Damariscotta, while groundfish still hold deep in Penobscot Bay.
body_markdown:
Forty years hauling traps off Monhegan and I can count on one hand the summers bluefish showed up thick enough in Boothbay Harbor to matter. This is one of them. I was running gear past The Cuckolds early last week, water slick and warm enough that it didn't sting my hands pulling wet warp, and there they were — a school of blues busting bait right off the mooring field, close enough that a fella on a Whaler was casting Kastmasters from his cockpit without even starting the engine. That's not normal water for this coast in mid-August, and it's not normal fish either. Old-timers in this harbor remember a handful of years like it, and they all说 the same thing — take advantage while it lasts, because Gulf of Maine warm pulses don't stick around.

We flagged this two weeks ago — said the snapper blues thick in the back bays and river mouths would keep building into adult-class fish through late August, and that's exactly what's happening in the Damariscotta and Sheepscot. The snappers that were finger-length in July are pushing 12 to 16 inches now, and mixed in are genuine 3- and 4-pound blues hitting topwater poppers and small metal off the mouth of the Damariscotta on the last two hours of the incoming tide. If you're throwing gear at them, keep it small — half-ounce Deadly Dicks or a 3-inch Slug-Go worked fast on top. They're not fussy, but they are moving fast through the current seams, so cover water instead of anchoring on one rip.

Striped bass are riding shotgun with that bait, same as they always do when mackerel and pogies stack up this thick. Eastern Egg Rock has been the most reliable striper water all week — the puffins are still working the surface bait balls out there, and where the birds are diving, there's usually a bass or two underneath cleaning up scraps. I've had the best luck working the western side of the rock on the last hour of the ebb, drifting live mackerel under a slip float, or working a white Deceiver through the froth when they're up on top. Fish have run mostly schoolies to 26 inches, with the occasional slot fish mixed in around dawn before the boat traffic picks up.

Mackerel themselves have been thick as I've seen them in a few seasons — Monhegan's ledges on the western side, in that 40 to 60 foot stretch off Manana, have been stacked with them most mornings on the last of the flood. A string of six mackerel jigs dropped straight down will load up fast, and that bait is exactly what's pulling the pollock up. Pollock have been breaking the surface at Monhegan in the evening light, working the edges where the current pinches around the ledges — cast a diamond jig or a 3-ounce Hopkins into the boil and let it flutter down through the school. Fish have run 3 to 8 pounds, with a couple pushing better than 10 taken on the troll working the drop-off east of the island.

Groundfish, meanwhile, are staying put right where they should be this time of year — deep, and out of the warm surface layer entirely. Cod and haddock are holding in the channels off Matinicus and in the deeper water east of Isle au Haut, 100 to 140 feet, and they want bait fished tight to bottom on the slower stages of the tide. Jigging with a diamond jig tipped with squid, or drifting clam bait on a high-low rig, has produced steady if not spectacular numbers — a mix of legal haddock to 24 inches and cod that are mostly shakers with a few keepers mixed in. It's not the kind of fishing where you fill a cooler fast, but it's honest work if you're willing to run the extra miles out past Vinalhaven and fish the deep water seriously.

Stonington and Deer Isle have been quieter than Egg Rock or Monhegan this week, which surprised me some given how good the tide lines usually set up through that thoroughfare in August. Wind out of the southwest most days kept things a little sloppy on the outer ledges, and the bass that were there seemed to slide off with the chop. If you're fishing that stretch, I'd work the lee side structure around Crotch Island on the last of the ebb, when the current settles and bait gets pinned against the rocks.

Tides are building back toward the full moon on the 28th, and that's going to matter. Bigger water means stronger current lines at Egg Rock and Monhegan, which should tighten up the bass and pollock bite around the ledges and give the mackerel schools somewhere firm to hold instead of scattering with every tide change. If this warm pulse holds through the week — and there's no sign yet it's breaking — I'd expect the bluefish push into Boothbay and the Damariscotta to keep building right along with it, maybe far enough to see them working past the Cuckolds and into outer Muscongus Bay by month's end. That would be something worth writing about. For now, my money's on Egg Rock at first light and Monhegan on the last of the flood — that's where I'm putting my own time this week, and I'd have a jig rod rigged for pollock just in case the mackerel show up thick again.
